readings.c1s2:
<poem>{{smaller block|Fowerti dais after this,
Arches ''windoge'' undon it is;
The Rauen ut-fleg, hu so it gan ben,
Ne cam he nogt to the arche a-gen.
{{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 60}}

My chambre was
Ful wel depeynted, and with glas
Were al the ''windowes'' wel y-glased,
Ful clere, and nat an hole y-crased.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 32}}}}</poem>
{{smaller block|The prentices made a riot upon my glass ''windows'' t Shrove-Tuesday following.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iv.}}}}
'''2.''' An aperture or opening resembling a wi dow or suggestive of a window.
{{smaller block|The ''windows'' of heaven. {{right|Gen. vii.}}

The ''window'' of my heart, mine eye.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 8}}}}
Hence —'''3.''' In ''anat.'', one of two holes in t inner wall of the tympanum, called respective the ''oval window'' and the ''round window'', fenest ovalis and fenestra rotunda. See ''fenestra.''—'''4.''' A cover; a lid.
{{smaller block|Ere I let fall the ''windows'' of mine eyes.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3. 1}}}}
'''5.''' A figure formed by lines crossing one a other.
<poem>{{smaller block|The Fav’rite child, that just begins to prattle, . .
Is very humorsome, and makes great clutter,
He has ''Windows'' on his Bread and Butter.
{{right|''W. King'', Art of Cooke}}}}</poem>
'''6†.''' A blank space.
{{smaller block|I will, therefore, that you send unto me a collati thereof; and that your said collation have a ''window'' pedient to set what name I will therein.
{{right|''Cranmer'', Works (Parker Soc.), II. 2}}}}
readings.c2s1:
—'''2.''' A bar of wood or iron for securing a window or the shutters of it when closed.—'''3.''' A horizontal bar fitted in a window or doorway, to prevent a child from falling through.—'''4.''' ''pl.'' Latticework, as on a woman’s stomacher. ''Shak.'', T. of A., iv. 3. 116.

'''window-blind''' (win′dō-blīnd), ''n.'' A blind, screen, or shade for a window. See ''blind''<sup>1</sup>.

'''window-bole''' (win′dō-bōl), ''n.'' Same as ''bole''<sup>4</sup>, 1.
{{smaller block|I was out on the ''window-bole'' when your auld back was turned, and awa’ down by to hae a baff at the popinjay.
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, vii.}}}}

'''window-curtain''' (win′dō-kėr″tạn), ''n.'' Same as ''curtain'', 1 (''b'').

'''window-frame''' (win′dō-frām), ''n.'' The frame of a window, which receives and holds the sashes.

'''window-gardening''' (win′dō-gärd″ning), ''n.'' The cultivation of plants indoors before a window.
{{smaller block|The boxes used in ''window-gardening'' are made of a great variety of materials, etc. ''Henderson'', Handbook of Plants.}}

'''window-gazer''' (win′dō-gā″zėr), ''n.'' An idler; one who gazes idly from a window.
readings.c2s2:
{{smaller block|Her sonnes gluttonous, her daughters ''window-gazers'',
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 304.}}}}

'''window-glass''' (win′dō-glȧs), ''n.'' Glass suitable for windows, or such as is commonly used for windows, especially the commoner kinds, as distinguished from plate-glass or other more costly varieties.—'''Spread window-glass.''' {{smaller|Same as ''broad glass'' (which see, under ''broad'').}}

'''window-jack''' (win′dō-jak), ''n.'' Same as ''builders’ jack'' (which see, under ''jack'').

'''window-latch''' (win′dō-lach), ''n.'' A catch or locking-device for holding a window-sash open or shut.

'''window-lead''' (win′dō-led), ''n.'' Same as ''came''<sup>3</sup>, 2.

'''windowless''' (win′dọ̄-les), ''a.'' [< ''window'' + ''-less.''] Destitute of windows.

{{smaller block|It is usual . . . to huddle them together into naked walls and ''windowless'' rooms.
{{right|''H. Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. 377. (''Davies.'')}}
I stood still at this end, which, being ''windowless'', was dark.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xvii.}}}}

'''windowlet''' (win′dọ̄-let), ''n.'' [< ''window'' + ''-let.''] A little window.

{{smaller block|<poem>If wak’d they cannot see, their eyes are blind,
Shut up like ''windolets.''</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', Solomon Paraphrased, xvii.}}}}

'''window-lift''' (win′dō-lift), ''n.'' A strap or a handle by which to raise a window-sash, especially in a carriage or a railway-car.

'''window-lock''' (win′dō-lok), ''n.'' A device for fastening the sash of a window so that it cannot be opened from the outside.

'''window-martin''' (win′dō-mär″tin), ''n.'' The common martin of Europe, ''Chelidon urbica''; the house-martin or window-swallow. See cut un-
readings.c2s3:
der ''martin.''

'''window-mirror''' (win′dō-mir″ọr), ''n.'' A mirror fastened outside of a window and adjustable at any angle, to reflect the image of objects in the street to the view of persons in the room, who may thus see without being seen.

'''window-opener''' (win′dō-ōp″nėr), ''n.'' A lever or rod by which a window, ventilator, sash, a panel in the raised roof of a railway-car, etc. may be opened and held in any desired position.

'''window-oyster''' (win′dō-ois″tėr), ''n.'' A bivalve mollusk of the family ''Placunidæ, Placuna placenta.'' Also ''window-shell.''

'''window-pane''' (win′dō-pān), ''n.'' '''1.''' One of the oblong or square plates of glass set in a window-frame.—'''2.''' The sand-flounder. [New Jersey.]

'''window-sash''' (win′dō-sash), ''n.'' The sash or light frame in which panes of glass are set for windows. See ''sash''<sup>1</sup>.

'''window-screen''' (win′dō-skrēn), ''n.'' Any device for filling all or part of the opening of a window, particularly if it is ornamental, as the pierced lattices of the Arabs; also, the glass filling of a stained or painted window.
{{smaller block|Chartres [cathedral], . . . singularly fortunate in retaining its magnificent jewel-like ''window-screens.''
{{right|''C. H. Moore,'' Gothic Architecture, p. 304.}}}}

'''window-seat''' (win′dō-sēt), ''n.'' A seat in the re
readings.c2s4:
cess of a window.

'''window-sector''' (win′dō-sek″tọr), ''n.'' A bar c plate of metal in the form of a sector of a circl used to control the movement and position c a window or ventilator in the raised roof of railway-car. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''window-shade''' (win′dō-shād), ''n.'' A contrivanc for shutting out or tempering light at a window a variety of window-blind, usually a piece c holland or similar material, arranged to roll u
readings.c3s1:
on a roller, and to cover the window when pulled out.

¶
'''window-shell''' (win′dō-shel), ''n.'' Same as ''window-oyster.''

'''window-shut†''' (win′dō-shut), ''n.'' A window-shutter.

{{smaller block|When you bar the ''window-shuts'' of your lady’s bed-chamber at nights, leave open the sashes.
{{right|''Swift,'' Advice to Servants (Chamber-maid).}}}}

'''window-shutter''' (win′dō-shut″ėr), ''n.'' A shutter used to darken or secure a window.

'''window-sill''' (win′dō-sil), ''n.'' The sill of a window. See ''sill''<sup>1</sup>, 1.

'''window-stile''' (win′dō-stīl), ''n.'' One of the vertical bars in a window-sash.

'''window-stool''' (win′dō-stöl), ''n.'' See ''stool.''

'''windowy†''' (win′dọ̄-i), ''a.'' [< ''window'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Exhibiting intersecting lines or little crossings like those of the sashes of a window.

{{smaller block|<poem>Poor fish, beset
With strangling snare, or ''windowy'' net.</poem>
{{right|''Donne,'' The Bait.}}}}

'''windpipe''' (wind′pīp), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''wyndpype''; < ''wind''<sup>2</sup> + ''pipe''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] The tube passing from the larynx to the division of the bronchi which conveys the air in respiration to and from the lungs. See ''trachea,'' and cut under ''mouth.''

'''wind-plant''' (wind′plant), ''n.'' The wind-flower, ''Anemone nemorosa.'' See cut under ''anemone.''

'''wind-pole''' (wind′pōl), ''n.'' See the quotation.

{{smaller block|Taking, with Dové, north-east and south-west (true) as the ''wind-poles,'' all intermediate directions are found to be more or less assimilated to the characteristics of those extremes, as they are nearer one or other.
{{right|''Fitz Roy,'' Weather Book, p. 173.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''wind-pox''' (wind′poks), ''n.'' Varicella or chicken-pox.

'''wind-pressure''' (wind′presh″ụ̄r), ''n.'' '''1.''' The pressure of the wind on any object in its path. {{smaller|The pressure of the wind blowing perpendicularly on a flat surface is usually deduced from its velocity by means of the equation <math>P = kAV^2</math>, where ''P'' is the pressure in pounds, ''V'' the velocity in feet per second, ''A'' the area of the surface in square feet, and ''k'' a numerical constant whose value for ordinary temperatures and barometric pressures is variously given from 0.0015 to 0.0022.}} '''2.''' In ''organ-building'', the degree of compression in the compressed air in the storage-bellows and the wind-chests.

'''wind-pump''' (wind′pump), ''n.'' A pump moved by wind.

'''wind-record''' (wind′rek″ọrd), ''n.'' A record of wind velocities or directions; especially, a continuous registration made by an anemograph or self-recording anemometer; an anemogram.

'''windring†''' (win′dring), ''a.'' [Possibly a misreading for ''winding'' or ''wandering''.] Winding.
{{smaller block|You nymphs, call’d Naiads, of the ''windring'' brooks.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 128.}}}}

'''wind-rode''' (wind′rōd), ''a.'' ''Naut.'', riding with head to wind instead of to current. Compare ''tide-rode''.

'''wind-root''' (wind′röt), ''n.'' The pleurisy-root, ''Asclepias tuberosa''.

'''wind-rose''' (wind′rōz), ''n.'' '''1.''' A table or diagram showing the relative frequency of winds blowing from the different points of the compass, or the relative amount of total wind-movement
readings.c3s3:
for each direction; also, a table or diagram showing the connection between the wind-direction and any other meteorological element: thus, a thermal ''wind-rose'' shows the average temperature prevailing with winds from different directions.—'''2.''' See ''rose''<sup>1</sup> and ''Rœmeria.''

'''windrow''' (wind′rō), ''n.'' [Also, corruptly, ''winrow;'' < ''wind''<sup>2</sup> + ''row''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''] '''1.''' A row or line of hay raked together for the purpose of being rolled into cocks or heaps; also, sheaves of corn set up in a row one against another in order that the wind may blow between them.—'''2.''' A row of peats set up for drying; a row of pieces of turf, sod, or sward cut in paring and burning.—'''3.''' Any similar row or formation; an extended heap, as of dust thrown up by the wind.
{{smaller block|Each day’s dust, before the next day came, was swept into ''windrows'' or whirled away altogether by intermittent gusts charging up the slope from the valley.
{{right|''The Century,'' XXXI. 63.}}}}
'''4.''' The green border of a field, dug up in order to carry the earth to other land to mend it: so called because laid in rows and exposed to the wind. ''Ray,'' Eng. Words (1691), p. 120.

'''windrow''' (wind′rō), ''v. t.'' [< ''windrow,'' ''n.''] To rake or put into the form of a windrow.

'''wind-sail''' (wind′sāl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A wide tube or funnel of canvas serving to convey a current of fresh air into the lower parts of a ship.—'''2.''' One of the vanes or sails of a windmill.—'''To trim a wind-sail,''' {{smaller|to turn the opening of the wind-sail toward the wind.}}

A table or diagram showing the relative frequency of winds blowing from the different points of the compass, or the relative amount of total wind-movement for each direction; also, a table or diagram showing the connection between the wind-direction and any other meteorological element: thus, a thermal ''wind-rose'' shows the average temperature prevailing with winds from different directions.—'''2.''' See ''rose''1 and ''Rœmeria.'' '''windrow''' (wind′rō), ''n.''   [Also, corruptly, ''winrow;'' < ''wind''2 + ''row''2, ''n.'']   '''1.''' A row or line of hay raked together for the purpose of being rolled into cocks or heaps; also, sheaves of corn set up in a row one against another in order that the wind may blow between them.—'''2.''' A row of peats set up for drying; a row of pieces of turf, sod, or sward cut in paring and burning.—'''3.''' Any similar row or formation; an extended heap, as of dust thrown up by the wind. {{smaller block|Each day’s dust, before the next day came, was swept into ''windrows'' or whirled away altogether by intermittent gusts charging up the slope from the valley. {{right|''The Century,'' XXXI. 63.}}}} '''4.''' The green border of a field, dug up in order to carry the earth to other land to mend it: so called because laid in rows and exposed to the wind.   ''Ray,'' Eng. Words (1691), p. 120. '''windrow''' (wind′rō), ''v. t.''   [< ''windrow,'' ''n.'']   To rake or put into the form of a windrow. '''wind-sail''' (wind′sāl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A wide tube or funnel of canvas serving to convey a current of fresh air into the lower parts of a ship.—'''2.''' One of the vanes or sails of a windmill.—'''To trim a wind-sail,''' {{smaller|to turn the opening of the wind-sail toward the wind.}}
